planting.note: Plant rooted offsets or container-grown plants in spring into very well-drained, dry, rocky or gravelly, alkaline soil in full sun; Faxon yucca is a slow-growing Trans-Pecos native that eventually forms a stout, tree-like trunk over many years.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, dry, rocky soil in full sun; Faxon yucca is a large, dramatic, tree-forming yucca of the Chihuahuan Desert and Trans-Pecos region, with stiff, dagger-like blue-green leaves crowded at the tips of one or more thick, woody trunks that develop slowly over decades of growth. A massive, densely packed flower spike of creamy white, waxy bell-shaped blooms rises several feet above the foliage in spring, one of the showiest floral displays of any cold-hardy desert plant. It is extremely drought and heat tolerant once established and tolerates winter cold well beyond what its desert origin suggests, needing only sharp drainage and full sun to thrive for many decades as a slow-growing architectural specimen. Give it plenty of room from walkways, since the rigid, spine-tipped leaves can cause painful puncture injuries on contact.

planting.note: Plant rooted offsets or container-grown plants in spring into very well-drained, dry, sandy soil in full sun; soaptree yucca, the New Mexico state flower, is native to Chihuahuan and Sonoran Desert grasslands and eventually forms a slender trunk with age.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, dry, sandy soil in full sun; soaptree yucca is the state flower of New Mexico, an iconic desert grassland plant with narrow, flexible, blue-green leaves edged in white, curling fibers that top a slender trunk which develops slowly over many decades, eventually reaching tree height in old specimens. A tall, arching flower stalk rises well above the foliage in late spring, densely packed with creamy white, bell-shaped flowers pollinated exclusively by the yucca moth in an obligate partnership found throughout the genus. The roots and trunk contain natural saponins historically used by Native American and Mexican communities as a soap and shampoo substitute, the source of its common name. It is exceptionally drought and heat tolerant, requiring virtually no supplemental water once established, and makes a striking, slow-growing architectural specimen for xeriscape and desert-style landscapes.

planting.note: Plant rooted offsets or container-grown plants in spring into very well-drained, dry, rocky or sandy, alkaline soil in full sun; banana yucca stays low and largely stemless, unlike its tree-forming relatives, spreading into a dense clump of offsets over time.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, dry, rocky soil in full sun; banana yucca forms a dense, largely stemless or low-trunked clump of thick, rigid, blue-green leaves and is notable among yuccas for producing a large, fleshy, banana-shaped fruit rather than the typical dry, papery capsule of most yucca species. A stout flower stalk of creamy white to purple-tinged bell-shaped blooms appears in late spring, followed by heavy green fruit that ripens to brown by late summer and was a significant traditional food source for Native American peoples of the Southwest, eaten fresh, dried, or baked once fully ripe and soft. It spreads slowly into a substantial multi-headed clump over the years and is exceptionally drought and cold tolerant, thriving in the same lean, rocky soils used by mountain mahogany and other tough Southwestern natives. Harvest fruit once it softens and begins to turn brown, and wear gloves when working near the sharp, rigid leaf tips.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring into very well-drained, dry, rocky or gravelly, alkaline soil in full sun; devil's shoestring forms a low, grass-like clump on limestone hills and canyon slopes of the Edwards Plateau region.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, dry, rocky soil in full sun; devil's shoestring is a Texas Hill Country native with a dense, fountain-like clump of narrow, tough, grass-like leaves that arch outward from a woody base rooted deep into limestone crevices and rocky slopes. A tall, wand-like flower spike lined with small cream-colored blooms rises above the foliage in late spring to early summer, adding vertical interest to a xeriscape or rock garden planting. Unlike its larger cousin, bear grass (Nolina texana), it stays compact and tidy, making it well suited to smaller rock gardens and dry border plantings where a bold yucca or agave might be too large. It thrives on pure neglect once established in appropriately lean, rocky soil, needing no fertilizer and only rare supplemental water during the most extreme droughts.

planting.note: Plant rooted offsets (pups) in spring into very well-drained, gritty, rocky, alkaline soil in full sun; New Mexico century plant is one of the most cold-hardy agave species, tolerating temperatures near 0°F once established in sharply drained soil.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, gritty, rocky soil in full sun; New Mexico century plant forms a compact, symmetrical rosette of thick, gray-green to blue-green leaves edged with small, closely spaced teeth and a sharp terminal spine, native to limestone hills and grasslands of the Chihuahuan Desert borderlands. It is remarkably cold-hardy for a true agave, tolerating hard freezes that would kill most other agave species, provided the soil drains sharply and the crown stays dry through winter. Like all agaves, it is monocarpic, spending a decade or more building the rosette before sending up a single tall, branched flower stalk once in its lifetime, after which the main rosette dies while offsets typically continue the clump. Water only sparingly to establish young plants, since overwatering in heavy or poorly drained soil is the most common cause of failure with this otherwise tough, long-lived species.

planting.note: Plant rooted offsets in spring into very well-drained, gritty, rocky, alkaline soil in full sun; rough agave is a Chihuahuan Desert native with distinctly rough-textured, gray-green leaves and moderate cold tolerance for the genus.

directions: Plant in very well-drained, gritty, rocky soil in full sun; rough agave forms a broad, symmetrical rosette of thick, gray-green leaves with a distinctly rough, sandpaper-like surface texture and reddish-brown marginal teeth, native to rocky hillsides and desert scrub of the Chihuahuan Desert. Its imposing rosette makes a strong architectural focal point in a xeriscape bed for years before the plant reaches flowering maturity, when it sends up a tall, branched flower stalk lined with yellow blooms in its single flowering event before the rosette dies. It is somewhat less cold-hardy than agaves like Agave neomexicana or Agave havardiana, so gardeners at the cooler edge of its range should site it in a protected, reflective location such as against a south-facing wall. Water only to establish, since mature specimens are extremely drought tolerant and prone to rot in heavy, slow-draining, or frequently irrigated soil.
